--- title: "Grouping & Aggregation" subtitle: "≈ `group_by()` + `summarise()` · `.by` · `reframe()` · `count()`" jupyter: python3 --- `group_by().agg()` is the context from [Expressions & Contexts](../core/expressions.qmd#sec-expr-contexts) where every expression runs once per group: a length-1 result becomes a value, anything longer becomes a list. This chapter builds on that rule: how keys are formed, the order groups come out in, which count counts what, how to pick one value per group, how to return several rows per group, and the `GroupBy` methods that skip `agg()`. ## In tidyverse {#sec-grp-tidyverse} From R4DS 2e, [Groups](https://r4ds.hadley.nz/data-transform.html#groups): ```r library(dplyr) library(nycflights13) flights |> group_by(month) |> summarize(avg_delay = mean(dep_delay, na.rm = TRUE), n = n()) flights |> summarize(delay = mean(dep_delay, na.rm = TRUE), n = n(), .by = c(origin, dest)) flights |> group_by(year, month, day) |> summarize(n = n()) # message: grouped by year, month ``` dplyr groups in two ways. `group_by()` returns a **grouped tibble**: the grouping persists, keys come out sorted, each `summarise()` peels off the last key (the `.groups` message), and you finish with `ungroup()`. `.by` groups for one verb only: keys come out in order of first appearance, and the result is never grouped. Polars has only the second kind. `group_by()` returns a `GroupBy` object that the next call consumes, and the result is a plain `DataFrame`: no grouped state, no `ungroup()`, no `.groups`. ::: {#90856644 .cell execution_count=2} ``` {.python .cell-code} import polars as pl from pl_notes import datasets flights_df = datasets.flights() penguins_df = datasets.penguins() flights_df.group_by("month").agg( avg_delay=pl.col("dep_delay").mean(), # skips nulls: na.rm = TRUE is the default n=pl.len(), ).sort("month").head(3) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=2} ```{=html}

``` ::: ::: Same numbers as R4DS (10.0 minutes over 27,004 flights in January). Without `.sort("month")` the months come out in arbitrary order (@sec-grp-order). ## Mental model {#sec-grp-model} ```text flights_df.group_by("month") a GroupBy: the frame + the keys, nothing computed yet ├── .agg(e1, e2, …) one row per group; each expression runs on each group ├── .len() .mean() … shortcut: one operation on every non-key column ├── .head(n) .tail(n) n whole rows per group ├── .having(predicate) drop whole groups (SQL HAVING); still a GroupBy ├── .map_groups(fn) a Python fn(sub_df) per group, results stacked └── for key, sub_df in … iterate; key is always a tuple Inside .agg(): split → apply → combine ┌─────────────┐ pl.col("dep_delay").mean() → 10.04 scalar │ month = 1 │──► pl.len() → 27004 scalar ──► one row: │ 27,004 rows │ pl.col("dep_delay") → [2, 4, …] list 1 │ 10.04 │ 27004 │ [2, 4, …] └─────────────┘ … and the same for month = 2, 3, … ``` A `GroupBy` holds only the frame and the keys (`.by`, `.maintain_order`). `.agg()` runs `df.lazy().group_by(...).agg(...).collect()`, so eager grouping goes through the same query engine as lazy code. | dplyr | Polars | |---|---| | `group_by(g)`: a grouped tibble that persists | `group_by("g")`: a `GroupBy`, used by the next call only | | `summarise()` drops one key (`.groups`); `ungroup()` | `agg()` returns a plain `DataFrame`; nothing to undo | | keys sorted (`group_by()`) or in first-appearance order (`.by`) | arbitrary; `.sort()` or `maintain_order=True` | | `group_by(g) |> filter(n() > k) |> summarise(...)` | `group_by("g").having(pl.len() > k).agg(...)` | | grouped `mutate()` / `filter()` | `expr.over("g")`, see [Window Functions](window.qmd) | : Grouping, side by side {.striped} ## Mechanics {#sec-grp-mechanics} ### Keys {#sec-grp-keys} Several keys go in as positional arguments, a list, or a selector (≈ `.by = c(origin, dest)`): ::: {#314b6b41 .cell execution_count=3} ``` {.python .cell-code} flights_df.group_by("origin", "dest", maintain_order=True).agg( delay=pl.col("dep_delay").mean(), n=pl.len() ).head(3) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=3} ```{=html}
shape: (3, 4)
origindestdelayn
strstrf64u32
"EWR""IAH"11.8265513973
"LGA""IAH"9.0589862951
"JFK""MIA"9.3365713314
``` ::: ::: A key can be an expression. A positional one keeps the name of its leftmost input (@sec-expr-naming), so this key is called `sched_dep_time` but holds hours: ::: {#d226a77e .cell execution_count=4} ``` {.python .cell-code} flights_df.group_by(pl.col("sched_dep_time") // 100).agg(pl.len()).sort("sched_dep_time").head(2) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=4} ```{=html}
shape: (2, 2)
sched_dep_timelen
i64u32
11
51953
``` ::: ::: Name computed keys with a keyword argument instead, e.g. `group_by(date=pl.col("time_hour").dt.date())` for R4DS's `group_by(year, month, day)`. Keyword keys come after the positional ones. Calendar buckets work the same way (`dt.truncate("1w")`); sliding and dynamic time windows (`group_by_dynamic()`, `rolling()`) belong to [Dates, Times & Durations](../types/datetime.qmd). A null key forms its own group, as in dplyr, and `sort()` puts it first (`penguins_df.group_by("sex").len().sort("sex")` gives null 11, female 165, male 168). Groups come only from rows that exist: an unused `Enum` level gets no row, and there is no `.drop = FALSE` (join onto the levels instead, see [Reshaping](reshape.qmd)). `agg()` with no expressions returns the distinct key combinations (≈ `distinct(species, island)`). Inside `agg()`, `pl.all()` means every **non-key** column, so `agg(pl.all().first())` does not duplicate the key. ### Output order and `maintain_order=` {#sec-grp-order} Groups are built by hashing the keys in parallel, so the default output order is arbitrary and changes between runs (two identical `group_by("dest")` calls on `flights` returned different orders). dplyr's two orders each have a Polars spelling: ::: {#bf7a6897 .cell execution_count=5} ``` {.python .cell-code} dest_df_first_seen = flights_df.group_by("dest", maintain_order=True).agg(n=pl.len()) # ≈ .by dest_df_sorted = flights_df.group_by("dest").agg(n=pl.len()).sort("dest") # ≈ group_by() dest_df_first_seen["dest"].head(4).to_list(), dest_df_sorted["dest"].head(4).to_list() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=5} ``` (['IAH', 'MIA', 'BQN', 'ATL'], ['ABQ', 'ACK', 'ALB', 'ANC']) ``` ::: ::: `maintain_order=True` means **first appearance**, not sorted. In the streaming engine's plan it adds a row index before the group-by and a sort of the *groups* by their first row after it: one sort over 105 groups, not 336,776 rows, which cost a few percent on `flights`. (The docstring says it blocks the streaming engine; on 2.0.0 the streaming engine ran it natively.) Within a group, rows always keep their input order, whatever `maintain_order` says. That is what makes `first()`, `last()` and `head()` meaningful: sort the frame, then group. ::: {#32d2659a .cell execution_count=6} ``` {.python .cell-code} flights_df.with_row_index("row").group_by("dest").agg( in_input_order=(pl.col("row").diff() > 0).all() ).select(pl.col("in_input_order").all()) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=6} ```{=html}
shape: (1, 1)
in_input_order

``` ::: ::: ### Counting {#sec-grp-count} | R | Polars | Nulls | |---|---|---| | `n()` | `pl.len()` | rows, nulls included | | `sum(!is.na(x))` | `pl.col("x").count()` | **excluded** | | `sum(is.na(x))` | `pl.col("x").null_count()` | only nulls | | `n_distinct(x)` | `pl.col("x").n_unique()` | null counts as one value | | `n_distinct(x, na.rm = TRUE)` | `pl.col("x").drop_nulls().n_unique()` | excluded | | `sum(x > 0, na.rm = TRUE)` | `(pl.col("x") > 0).sum()` | null comparisons skipped | : Which count counts what {.striped} Cancelled flights have a null `dep_time`, and a few have no `tailnum`: ::: {#b43f197e .cell execution_count=7} ``` {.python .cell-code} flights_df.group_by("month").agg( n=pl.len(), n_departed=pl.col("dep_time").count(), n_cancelled=pl.col("dep_time").null_count(), n_planes=pl.col("tailnum").n_unique(), n_planes_known=pl.col("tailnum").drop_nulls().n_unique(), ).sort("month").head(3) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=7} ```{=html}

``` ::: ::: Every count is `UInt32` ([Counts are unsigned](../core/data-model.qmd#sec-dm-unsigned)), including the sum of a Boolean (@sec-grp-unsigned). The rest of the `count()` family, beyond the cheatsheet's rows ([Summarise & Group](../overview/polars-cheatsheet.qmd#sec-cs-summarise)): | dplyr | Polars | |---|---| | `tally()` | `df.select(n=pl.len())`, or `df.height` | | `count(g, wt = x)` | `df.group_by("g").agg(n=pl.col("x").sum())` | | `count(g, name = "k")` | `df.group_by("g").len(name="k")` | | `count(g) |> mutate(prop = n / sum(n))` | `df["g"].value_counts(normalize=True)`: column `proportion` | | `summarise(across(everything(), \(x) sum(!is.na(x))))` | `df.count()` | : The `count()` family; `value_counts()` on an expression returns a struct (@sec-grp-reframe) {.striped} ### Picking one value per group {#sec-grp-pick} Beyond the cheatsheet's `first()` / `last()` / `get()`: | dplyr | Polars | Note | |---|---|---| | `first(x, na_rm = TRUE)` | `.first(ignore_nulls=True)` | also `last()` and the `GroupBy` shortcuts | | `nth(x, -1)` | `.get(-1)` | negative counts from the end | | `nth(x, 100)` past the end → `NA` | `.get(99, null_on_oob=True)` | without it, out of range is an error | | `x[which.max(y)]` | `pl.col("x").get(pl.col("y").arg_max())` | | | assert one value | `.item()` | error unless exactly one; `allow_empty=True` → null | : Picking values {.striped} `pl.nth(1)` is not `nth(x, 2)`: it selects the second *column* of the frame. **The value of `x` at the maximum of `y`** has four spellings, and they differ on nulls: ::: {#6cd82f0d .cell execution_count=8} ``` {.python .cell-code} toy_df = pl.DataFrame({"g": ["a", "a", "a", "b"], "x": ["p", "q", "r", "s"], "y": [3, None, 5, None]}) toy_df.group_by("g", maintain_order=True).agg( sort_last=pl.col("x").sort_by("y").last(), sort_desc_first=pl.col("x").sort_by("y", descending=True).first(), # trap sort_desc_nl=pl.col("x").sort_by("y", descending=True, nulls_last=True).first(), at_arg_max=pl.col("x").get(pl.col("y").arg_max()), top_k_by=pl.col("x").top_k_by("y", 1).first(), ) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=8} ```{=html}
shape: (2, 6)

"a""r""q""r""r""r"
"b""s""s""s"null"s"
``` ::: ::: - `sort_by()` puts nulls first, like `sort()`. Sorting descending and taking `first()` returns the null row (`q`). Use `nulls_last=True`, or ascending + `last()`. - `arg_max()` ignores nulls, so an all-null group gives null (`b`). The others return the null row. - `top_k_by("y", k)` returns *k* values, a list inside `agg()` until `.first()` makes it a scalar. - **Ties:** none of them picks a defined row. `sort_by()` is unstable unless `maintain_order=True`, and the docs of `arg_max()` and `top_k_by()` say a tie is broken arbitrarily. To keep every tied row, see @sec-grp-recipes. A multi-column expression takes several columns from the same row: on `flights`, `pl.col("carrier", "flight", "dest").top_k_by("arr_delay", 1).first()` per `origin` returns the worst-delayed flight's carrier, number and destination. ### Conditional aggregation {#sec-grp-conditional} A `.filter()` inside one expression affects only that expression: `late_avg` sees late flights only, while `n` sees all of them. A frame-level `filter()` before grouping would change every column. ::: {#3761d255 .cell execution_count=9} ``` {.python .cell-code} flights_df.group_by("carrier").agg( n=pl.len(), prop_late=(pl.col("arr_delay") > 0).mean(), # nulls skipped late_avg=pl.col("arr_delay").filter(pl.col("arr_delay") > 0).mean(), n_very_late=(pl.col("arr_delay") > 120).sum(), ).sort("prop_late", descending=True).head(3) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=9} ```{=html}

To drop whole groups, use `having()`, SQL's `HAVING`: its predicates are aggregations evaluated per group and combined with `&`. ::: {#3a85d32b .cell execution_count=11} ``` {.python .cell-code} flights_df.group_by("dest").having(pl.len() > 15000).agg( n=pl.len(), delay=pl.col("arr_delay").mean() ).sort("dest") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=11} ```{=html}

To keep the *rows* of the big groups instead, use `filter(pl.len().over("dest") > 15000)` ([Window Functions](window.qmd)). ### Quantiles and medians {#sec-grp-quantiles} ::: {#8e02dca6 .cell execution_count=12} ``` {.python .cell-code} pl.DataFrame({"x": [1.0, 2.0, 3.0, 4.0]}).select( median=pl.col("x").median(), q25=pl.col("x").quantile(0.25), # default "nearest" q25_linear=pl.col("x").quantile(0.25, interpolation="linear"), ) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=12} ```{=html}
shape: (1, 3)
medianq25q25_linear
f64f64f64
2.52.01.75
``` ::: ::: `median()` matches R. `quantile()` does not: R's default (type 7) is linear interpolation, `quantile(1:4, 0.25)` = 1.75, while Polars defaults to `"nearest"`. Pass `interpolation="linear"` to match R. The other methods are `"higher"`, `"lower"`, `"midpoint"` and `"equiprobable"`. A list of probabilities works in `select()` but not in `agg()` or `over()`. The workaround, one scalar quantile per probability packed into a list, is in the next section. ::: {#f2c98a7d .cell execution_count=13} ``` {.python .cell-code} penguins_df.group_by("species").agg(pl.col("body_mass_g").quantile([0.25, 0.5, 0.75])) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-error} ::: {.ansi-escaped-output} ```{=html} 
SchemaError: expected expression of dtype 'numeric' for quantile, got 'list[f64]'

This error occurred in the following expression:
	col("body_mass_g").quantile([[0.25, 0.5, 0.75]])
``` ::: ::: ::: ### Several rows per group: `reframe()` {#sec-grp-reframe} ```r penguins |> reframe( prob = c(0.25, 0.5, 0.75), mass = quantile(body_mass_g, c(0.25, 0.5, 0.75), na.rm = TRUE), .by = species ) ``` `agg()` stores a multi-value result as a list, and `explode()` turns lists into rows, so `reframe()` ≈ `agg()` + `explode()`: ::: {#bb5a37a7 .cell execution_count=14} ``` {.python .cell-code} probs = [0.25, 0.5, 0.75] penguins_df.group_by("species", maintain_order=True).agg( prob=pl.lit(probs), mass=pl.concat_list( [pl.col("body_mass_g").quantile(p, interpolation="linear") for p in probs] ), ).explode("prob", "mass") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=14} ```{=html}

Without groups, `select()` with equal-length outputs is already `reframe()` (@sec-expr-contexts). Some expressions return several *columns* at once, as a struct. `value_counts()` returns one struct per distinct value, so inside `agg()` you get a list of structs: explode to rows, then unnest to columns. ::: {#02036014 .cell execution_count=15} ``` {.python .cell-code} penguins_df.group_by("species", maintain_order=True).agg( pl.col("island").value_counts(sort=True) ).explode("island").unnest("island") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=15} ```{=html}

``` ::: ::: ### Shortcuts on `GroupBy` {#sec-grp-shortcuts} | Method | Same as | Note | |---|---|---| | `.len(name="n")` | `.agg(n=pl.len())` | `GroupBy.count()` was removed in 2.0 | | `.first()`, `.last()` | `.agg(pl.all().first())` | `ignore_nulls=` | | `.sum()`, `.mean()`, `.median()`, `.min()`, `.max()`, `.n_unique()` | `.agg(pl.all().mean())`, … | every non-key column | | `.quantile(q)` | `.agg(pl.all().quantile(q))` | `"nearest"` by default | | `.all()` | `.agg(pl.all())` | every column as a list | | `.head(n)`, `.tail(n)` | `slice_head(n =)`, `slice_tail(n =)` | rows, not lists; `n=5` by default | | `.having(...)` | | returns a `GroupBy` | | `.map_groups(fn)` | `group_modify()` | Python per group (@sec-grp-escape) | : `GroupBy` methods in 2.0 (no `std()`, `var()` or `count()`: use `agg()`) {.striped} A shortcut applies to every non-key column, whatever its dtype. `mean()` of a string column is null, with no warning: ::: {#fddc66e8 .cell execution_count=16} ``` {.python .cell-code} penguins_df.group_by("species", maintain_order=True).mean() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=16} ```{=html}

AttributeRemovedError: `count` was removed in version 2.0; `GroupBy.count` was renamed; use `GroupBy.len` instead.
``` ::: ::: ::: ### Escape hatches: split, iterate, apply {#sec-grp-escape} `partition_by()` ≈ `group_split()`. With `as_dict=True` the keys are tuples, even for one key column. Unlike `group_by()`, it keeps first-appearance order by default, and it takes column names or selectors, not expressions (add a derived key with `with_columns()` first): ::: {#368f8a73 .cell execution_count=18} ``` {.python .cell-code} penguins_by_species = penguins_df.partition_by("species", as_dict=True) list(penguins_by_species), penguins_by_species[("Gentoo",)].shape ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=18} ``` ([('Adelie',), ('Gentoo',), ('Chinstrap',)], (124, 8)) ``` ::: ::: Iterating over a `GroupBy` yields `(key_tuple, sub_df)` pairs: ::: {#0ae7760c .cell execution_count=19} ``` {.python .cell-code} for (species,), species_df in penguins_df.group_by("species", maintain_order=True): print(f"{species:<10} {species_df.height:>4} rows") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Adelie 152 rows Gentoo 124 rows Chinstrap 68 rows ``` ::: ::: `map_groups(fn)` calls a Python function on each sub-frame and stacks the returned frames, like `group_modify()`. It is the last resort: Python per group, no parallelism, no query optimization. ::: {#4b8702b2 .cell execution_count=20} ``` {.python .cell-code} import numpy as np def fit_slope(species_df: pl.DataFrame) -> pl.DataFrame: """Least-squares slope of body mass on flipper length (g per mm).""" complete_df = species_df.drop_nulls(["flipper_length_mm", "body_mass_g"]) slope, _ = np.polyfit(complete_df["flipper_length_mm"], complete_df["body_mass_g"], 1) return pl.DataFrame({"species": complete_df["species"][:1], "slope": [slope]}) penguins_df.group_by("species", maintain_order=True).map_groups(fit_slope) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=20} ```{=html}

``` ::: ::: ## Where it bites {#sec-grp-gotchas} | tidyverse behaviour | Polars behaviour | |---|---| | `group_by()` output is sorted by key | arbitrary order: `.sort()` or `maintain_order=True` | | `count()` counts rows per group | `count()` counts **non-null** values; rows per group is `len()` | | an unaggregated column in `summarise()` warns | it silently becomes a list column | | `n()` and `sum(x > 0)` are signed | `UInt32`: differences wrap around | | `nth(x, 2)` | `pl.nth(1)` is the second column; use `.get(1)` | | `quantile()` interpolates (type 7) | `"nearest"` by default; a list of probabilities fails in `agg()` | | `slice_max()` keeps ties | `top_k_by()`, `arg_max()` and unstable sorts pick one tied row arbitrarily | | `.drop = FALSE` keeps empty factor levels | empty groups never appear, even for an `Enum` | | `group_split()` returns a list | iteration and `partition_by(as_dict=True)` keys are tuples | : The differences at a glance {.striped} `count` never means dplyr's `count()`: `Expr.count()` counts non-null values, `DataFrame.count()` does that for every column (`penguins_df.count()` gives 342 for `body_mass_g`, not 344), and `GroupBy.count()` is gone (@sec-grp-shortcuts). ### Forgetting to aggregate gives a list column {#sec-grp-list-trap} The list-or-scalar decision is **static**: it comes from the expression, not from the data. `head(1)` changes length, so it yields a list even though every list holds one value. `first()` aggregates, so it yields a scalar: ::: {#fda61d1b .cell execution_count=22} ``` {.python .cell-code} penguins_df.group_by("species").agg( head_1=pl.col("body_mass_g").head(1), first=pl.col("body_mass_g").first() ).schema ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=22} ``` Schema([('species', String), ('head_1', List(Int64)), ('first', Int64)]) ``` ::: ::: A forgotten aggregation does not fail where you made it. Arithmetic on a list column works element-wise, so the error surfaces later, at a comparison: ::: {#7ef43281 .cell execution_count=23} ``` {.python .cell-code} delays_df = flights_df.group_by("dest").agg(delay=pl.col("arr_delay")) # forgot .mean() delays_df.with_columns(pl.col("delay") / 60).filter(pl.col("delay") > 1) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-error} ::: {.ansi-escaped-output} ```{=html} 
SchemaError: could not evaluate '>' comparison between series 'delay' of dtype: List(Float64) and series 'literal' of dtype: Int32

This error occurred in the following expression:
	[(col("delay")) > (dyn int: 1)]
``` ::: ::: ::: Check `.schema` after an `agg()`: an unexpected `list[...]` is a missing aggregation. ### Boolean counts are unsigned {#sec-grp-unsigned} The sum of a Boolean is a count, so it is `UInt32` too, and subtracting a larger count wraps around. Cast to `Int64` before subtracting (more in [Counts are unsigned](../core/data-model.qmd#sec-dm-unsigned)): ::: {#cbbd488d .cell execution_count=24} ``` {.python .cell-code} flights_df.group_by("origin").agg( n_late=(pl.col("dep_delay") > 0).sum(), n_early=(pl.col("dep_delay") < 0).sum() ).with_columns(late_minus_early=pl.col("n_late") - pl.col("n_early")).sort("origin") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=24} ```{=html}

``` ::: ::: `pl.col("carrier").value_counts(sort=True, normalize=True)` inside `agg()` gives the same proportions in one step. **Top row per group, with or without ties** (≈ `slice_max()`). R4DS runs `flights |> group_by(dest) |> slice_max(arr_delay, n = 1)` and gets 108 rows for 105 destinations: ::: {#2c0d1808 .cell execution_count=26} ``` {.python .cell-code} worst_df_ties = flights_df.filter(pl.col("arr_delay") == pl.col("arr_delay").max().over("dest")) worst_df_head = ( flights_df.sort("arr_delay", descending=True, nulls_last=True).group_by("dest").head(1) ) worst_df_topk = ( flights_df.group_by("dest").agg(pl.all().top_k_by("arr_delay", 1)).explode(pl.exclude("dest")) ) { "filter == max().over() (ties kept)": worst_df_ties.height, "sort + group_by().head(1)": worst_df_head.height, "agg(top_k_by) + explode": worst_df_topk.height, } ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=26} ``` {'filter == max().over() (ties kept)': 107, 'sort + group_by().head(1)': 105, 'agg(top_k_by) + explode': 105} ``` ::: ::: These counts account for R4DS's 108. 104 destinations have a maximum and three of them (CHS, ILM, RSW) have a tie, which gives 107 rows. The 108th is LGA's only flight, whose `arr_delay` is null: `slice_max()` keeps it, while the `filter()` drops it because `null == null` is null. The other two methods return one row per destination, LGA included, and break ties arbitrarily. For the top *n* by rank, use `rank().over()` ([Window Functions](window.qmd)). **Random rows per group** (≈ `slice_sample(n = 2)`): shuffle once with a seed, then take the head of each group, which keeps the shuffled order: `df.sample(fraction=1, shuffle=True, seed=42).group_by("g").head(2)`. **Collapse a group's values into one string** (≈ `paste(sort(unique(carrier)), collapse = ", ")`): ::: {#b1f0be01 .cell execution_count=27} ``` {.python .cell-code} with pl.Config(fmt_str_lengths=60): # show the full strings print(flights_df.group_by("origin").agg( n_carriers=pl.col("carrier").n_unique(), carriers=pl.col("carrier").unique().sort().str.join(", "), ).sort("origin")) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` shape: (3, 3) ┌────────┬────────────┬────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │ origin ┆ n_carriers ┆ carriers │ │ --- ┆ --- ┆ --- │ │ str ┆ u32 ┆ str │ ╞════════╪════════════╪════════════════════════════════════════════════════╡ │ EWR ┆ 12 ┆ 9E, AA, AS, B6, DL, EV, MQ, OO, UA, US, VX, WN │ │ JFK ┆ 10 ┆ 9E, AA, B6, DL, EV, HA, MQ, UA, US, VX │ │ LGA ┆ 13 ┆ 9E, AA, B6, DL, EV, F9, FL, MQ, OO, UA, US, WN, YV │ └────────┴────────────┴────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ ``` ::: ::: `str.join()` aggregates, so the result is a scalar.
